If \(y=y(x)\) and it follows the relation \(x\cos y+y\cos x=\pi\), then \(y''(0)=\)
questions.sol: At \(x=0\): \(y=\pi\). First derivative: \(\cos y-x\sin y\,y'+y'\cos x-y\sin x=0\) gives \(y'(0)=1\). Differentiating again and putting \(x=0\), \(y=\pi\), \(y'=1\): \(-2\sin\pi+y''-\pi=0\).

Let \(f(x)=x\sin\pi x\), \(x>0\). Then for all natural numbers \(n\), \(f'(x)\) vanishes at
opts: a unique point in the interval \(\left(n,n+\dfrac12\right)\)
a unique point in the interval \(\left(n+\dfrac12,n+1\right)\)
a unique point in the interval \((n,n+1)\)
questions.sol: \(f'=\sin\pi x+\pi x\cos\pi x=0\) means \(\tan\pi x=-\pi x<0\). In \((n,n+1)\), \(\tan\pi x\) is negative only on \(\left(n+\frac12,n+1\right)\), where it increases from \(-\infty\) to \(0\) while \(-\pi x\) decreases: exactly one crossing.

questions.q: Differentiate from first principle (or ab initio) \(\sin(x^2+1)\).
If \(f(x)=x\tan^{-1}x\), find \(f'(1)\) from first principle.
Given \(y=\dfrac{5x}{3\sqrt{(1-x)^2}}+\cos^2(2x+1)\), find \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\)
questions.sol: \(\sqrt{(1-x)^2}=|1-x|\). For \(x<1\): \(\dfrac d{dx}\dfrac{5x}{3(1-x)}=\dfrac5{3(1-x)^2}\); for \(x>1\) the sign changes. \(\dfrac d{dx}\cos^2(2x+1)=-2\sin(4x+2)\).

questions.q: Let \(y=e^{x\sin x^3}+(\tan x)^x\) find \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\)
questions.sol: \(\dfrac d{dx}(x\sin x^3)=\sin x^3+3x^3\cos x^3\). For \(u=(\tan x)^x\): \(\dfrac{u'}u=\log\tan x+\dfrac{x\sec^2x}{\tan x}=\log\tan x+2x\,\text{cosec}\,2x\).

questions.q: Find the derivative with respect to \(x\) of the function \(y=\left\{\log_{\cos x}\sin x\left(\log_{\sin x}\cos x\right)^{-1}\right\}+\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}\right)\) at \(x=\dfrac\pi4\)
questions.sol: The first part is \(u=\left(\dfrac{\ln\sin x}{\ln\cos x}\right)^2\), with \(u'=2\cdot\dfrac{\ln\sin x}{\ln\cos x}\cdot\dfrac{\cot x\ln\cos x+\tan x\ln\sin x}{(\ln\cos x)^2}\). At \(\frac\pi4\), \(\ln\sin x=\ln\cos x=L=-\frac12\ln2\): \(u'=\dfrac4L=-\dfrac8{\ln2}\). The second part is \(2\tan^{-1}x\) (as \(x<1\)), with derivative \(\dfrac2{1+\pi^2/16}\).

questions.q: Find \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) at \(x=-1\), if \((\sin y)^{\sin\left(\frac\pi2x\right)}+\dfrac{\sqrt3}2\sec^{-1}(2x)+2^x\tan(\ln(x+2))=0\)
questions.sol: At \(x=-1\): \(\dfrac1{\sin y}+\dfrac{\sqrt3}2\cdot\dfrac{2\pi}3=0\), so \(\sin y=-\dfrac{\sqrt3}\pi\). Differentiating at \(x=-1\): the first term gives \(-\dfrac{\cos y}{\sin^2y}y'\) (as \(\cos\frac{\pi x}2=0\), \(\sin\frac{\pi x}2=-1\)), the second \(\dfrac{\sqrt3}2\cdot\dfrac2{2\sqrt3}=\dfrac12\), the third \(\dfrac12\). So \(y'=\dfrac{\sin^2y}{\cos y}=\dfrac{3/\pi^2}{\sqrt{\pi^2-3}/\pi}\) (taking \(\cos y>0\)).

questions.q: If \(y=\dfrac{ax^2}{(x-a)(x-b)(x-c)}+\dfrac{bx}{(x-b)(x-c)}+\dfrac c{(x-c)}+1\), prove that \(\dfrac{y'}y=\dfrac1x\left(\dfrac a{a-x}+\dfrac b{b-x}+\dfrac c{c-x}\right)\)
questions.sol: Combine from the right: \(\dfrac c{x-c}+1=\dfrac x{x-c}\); adding \(\dfrac{bx}{(x-b)(x-c)}\) gives \(\dfrac{x^2}{(x-b)(x-c)}\); adding the first term gives \(y=\dfrac{x^3}{(x-a)(x-b)(x-c)}\). Then \(\dfrac{y'}y=\dfrac3x-\sum\dfrac1{x-a}=\sum\left(\dfrac1x-\dfrac1{x-a}\right)=\dfrac1x\sum\dfrac a{a-x}\). (The book prints the third term as \(\frac x{x-c}\).)

Let \(f(x)=2+\cos x\) for all real \(x\).
Statement-1 : For each real \(t\), there exists a point \(c\) in \([t,t+\pi]\) such that \(f'(c)=0\).
Statement-2 : \(f(t)=f(t+2\pi)\) for each real \(t\).
opts: Statement-1 is True, Statement-2 is True; Statement-2 is a correct explanation of Statement-1
Statement-1 is True, Statement-2 is True; Statement-2 is NOT a correct explanation for Statement-1
Statement-1 is True, Statement-2 is False
Statement-1 is False, Statement-2 is True.
questions.sol: \(f'(x)=-\sin x\) vanishes at every multiple of \(\pi\), and every closed interval of length \(\pi\) contains one: Statement-1 is true. Statement-2 (period \(2\pi\)) is true but does not explain an interval of length \(\pi\).

questions.q: If the function \(f(x)=x^3+e^{\frac x2}\) and \(g(x)=f^{-1}(x)\), then the value of \(g'(1)\) is

Let \(\mathbb R\) denote the set of all real numbers. Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) and \(g:\mathbb R\to(0,4)\) be functions defined by \(f(x)=\log_e(x^2+2x+4)\), and \(g(x)=\dfrac4{1+e^{-2x}}\).
Define the composite function \(f\circ g^{-1}\) by \((f\circ g^{-1})(x)=f(g^{-1}(x))\), where \(g^{-1}\) is the inverse of the function \(g\).
Then the value of the derivative of the composite function \(f\circ g^{-1}\) at \(x=2\) is ______.
questions.sol: \(g(0)=2\), so the derivative is \(\dfrac{f'(0)}{g'(0)}\). \(f'(0)=\dfrac24=\dfrac12\) and \(g'(0)=\dfrac{8e^0}{(1+1)^2}=2\): value \(\dfrac14\).

questions.q:
Let \(\mathbb R\) denote the set of all real numbers. Consider the polynomial function \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) defined by \(f(x)=\dfrac{d^{10}}{dx^{10}}\left((x^2-1)^{10}\right)\), for all \(x\in\mathbb R\).
Here \(\dfrac{d^{10}}{dx^{10}}\left((x^2-1)^{10}\right)\) is the \(10^{\text{th}}\) order derivative of the function \((x^2-1)^{10}\).
Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE ?
opts: The coefficient of \(x^8\) in the polynomial \(f(x)\) is \((-10)\left(\dfrac{18!}{8!}\right)\)
The value of \(f(1)+f(-1)\) is equal to \(10!\,2^{11}\)
The degree of the polynomial \(f(x)\) is \(10\)
The constant term of the polynomial \(f(x)\) is \(-\left(\dfrac{10!}{5!}\right)\)
